evidence.current:
Alexander presents a pragmatic-prudential argument for accepting free will, using key Greek terms: πρακτέον (prakteon, one must act), ἀσφαλέστερον (asphalesteron, safer), κίνδυνος (kindynos, risk/danger).

Argument structure:
Premise 1: If determinism is true and we believe in free will, we lose nothing (our actions were fated anyway)
Premise 2: If free will is true and we believe in determinism, we risk moral disaster (abandoning responsibility)
Premise 3: It is rational to minimize risk of catastrophic outcomes
Conclusion: It is pragmatically safer (ἀσφαλέστερον) to believe in free will

This anticipates Pascal's Wager by ~1400 years, applied to metaphysics rather than theology. Alexander argues that even if we cannot resolve the theoretical question, practical reason dictates acceptance of free will. One of the earliest known "pragmatic" arguments in ancient philosophy - reasoning from practical consequences rather than theoretical proof.

proposed_action: In De Fato 36 Alexander turns the determinists' own act of arguing against them. He grants that if the determinists are compelled by surrounding causes (αἴτια περιεστῶτα) to assert their thesis, they deserve pardon (συγγινώσκειν αὐτοῖς ἄξιον) and there is no point disputing with them, since the cause of everything said and believed would be 'the power of the surrounding circumstances'. But if instead we have the power (ἐξουσίαν ἔχομεν) to say something better or worse, this already shows that something is up to us (ἐφ' ἡμῖν). The argument is thus a self-refutation charge against the determinist's act of reasoned assertion, not a prudential 'wager'.

evidence.issue: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite is a genuinely anonymous author whose actual birth and death dates are unknown. The only dateable fact is the floruit / composition date c. 500 CE (the Corpus Areopagiticum is dated c. 500 via its dependence on Proclus). Setting both birth_date and death_date to 'c. 500 CE' falsely implies known biographical dates and a near-zero lifespan, when scholarship uniformly treats c. 500 CE as a floruit, not as birth/death years.
evidence.rationale: The scanner is correct. Authoritative scholarship (IEP, SEP, Britannica) is unanimous that the author is anonymous with unknown birth/death dates, and that c. 500 CE is a floruit/composition date, not a lifespan. Encoding identical birth_date=death_date='c. 500 CE' is a false-fact: it asserts biographical dates that are not known and implies an impossible ~0-year life. The grounded correction is to null both fields; the floruit remains accurately represented in the description. Fix is scholarly (factual content), severity medium (imprecise/false but on a node where the floruit itself is correct and prominently stated).

evidence.evidence: Description: 'Critical edition: W. Jaeger, GNO I (Books I and II; 1921, rev. 1960), GNO II (Book III; 1925, rev. 1960; Brill 1990 reprint). English: S.G. Hall (in NPNF 2.5; ...).' Internet Archive scan 'contraeunomiumli02greg' (= GNO II Pars Altera) bears the imprint 'Berolini: Apud Weidmannos, 1921'. NPNF 2.5 'Against Eunomius' translators = Moore/Wilson/Ogle (CCEL npnf205; New Advent 2901).
evidence.issue: Two distinct bibliographic errors in the same description string. (A) [this pass] GNO vol. II (Pars Altera = Contra Eunomium Liber III + Refutatio Confessionis Eunomii) is dated '1925'; its editio princeps was Berlin: Weidmann 1921, concurrent with GNO vol. I (Books I-II, also 1921), revised 1960 (Brill, Leiden), with a later 1990 Brill reprint — there was no intermediate 1925 edition. (B) [prior pass, retained] The NPNF 2nd ser. vol. 5 English translation of Against Eunomius is attributed to S.G. Hall, but the actual NPNF 2.5 translators were W. Moore, H.A. Wilson, and H.C. Ogle (ed. Schaff-Wace, 1893); Hall's translation is the modern Brill Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae colloquium volumes, a distinct series.
evidence.rationale: Both sub-claims independently confirmed against primary metadata, not memory. (A) GNO II date: Internet Archive scan 'contraeunomiumli02greg' carries the title-page imprint 'Berolini: Apud Weidmannos, 1921'; Brill GNO serial page, HathiTrust, abebooks, and the Rutgers DBCS Jaeger biography all give 1921 (Berlin) as the editio princeps of GNO I and II, with the 1960 second edition by Brill (Leiden). No 1925 edition of this volume exists; the date is a single-token error. (B) NPNF translators: CCEL npnf205 and New Advent 2901 attribute 'Against Eunomius' to W. Moore, H.A. Wilson, H.C. Ogle (1893); S.G. Hall is the translator in Brill's Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae (CE II = SVC 82, 2007; CE III = SVC 124, 2014; CE I = SVC 148, 2018). The two series are conflated. Both corrections are grounded and warrant a scholarly fix; fix_class=scholarly governs the merged finding.

evidence.evidence: current text: '71 sections (counting Ambigua 6–71 in the traditional numbering; preceded by Ambigua ad Thomam, 5 sections)'. The same sentence already states the predecessor work has 5 sections (Ambigua 1–5 = ad Thomam), so the ad Iohannem necessarily spans Amb. 6–71 = 66 difficulties. The standard structure (Amb. 1–5 = ad Thomam; Amb. 6–71 = ad Iohannem) is the uncontested numbering used in the Constas critical edition (Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library 28–29, Harvard 2014).
evidence.issue: The description states '71 sections (counting Ambigua 6–71 in the traditional numbering)'. Counting the difficulties numbered 6 through 71 yields 66 sections (71 − 6 + 1 = 66), not 71. The figure 71 is the highest ambiguum number in the combined corpus (Ambigua ad Thomam 1–5 + Ambigua ad Iohannem 6–71), not the count of sections in the Ambigua ad Iohannem. The current phrasing is internally contradictory.
evidence.rationale: Arithmetic is unambiguous: difficulties numbered 6 through 71 inclusive = 66 sections. The combined Ambigua corpus comprises the Ambigua ad Thomam (Amb. 1–5) plus the Ambigua ad Iohannem (Amb. 6–71); this two-part structure with the 5 + 66 split is standard in Maximian scholarship and in the Constas edition cited in the node itself. The '71' refers to the last ambiguum number, not the section count. The node already correctly states the ad Thomam has 5 sections, making the '71' figure self-contradictory. Correction is grounded in the edition already cited; no ancient text composed.
sources: Nicholas Constas (ed./trans.), On Difficulties in the Church Fathers: The Ambigua, Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library 28–29 (Harvard University Press, 2014) — vol. I = Ambigua ad Thomam + Ambigua ad Iohannem 1–22; vol. II = Ambigua to John 23–71
